Administrators implement statutes both by adjudicating disputes and 
by promulgating general rules of conduct. Administrative implementation 
through rulemaking poses special problems—^both of political and legal 
accountability and of process fairness. What are the appropriate 
substantive checks on administrators’ rulemaking discretion? What 
procedures should agencies be required to follow when they are in 
legislative, or quasi-legislative mode?
Answers to these questions are not to be found in the jurisprudence 
governing judicial review of legislation. Judges are notoriously tolerant of 
asserted procedural errors by the legislature. A famous nineteenth century 
case, Marshall Field & Co, v, Clark, 143 U.S. 649 (1892), enunciates the 
“enrolled bill” rule: The courts will not entertain a claim that the 
Constitution’s procedures for the enactment of laws were not observed 
unless proof of the defect appears on the face of the statute (“enrolled bill”) 
filed with the Secretary of State. This doctrine has no counterpart in 
jj
judicial review of agency rulemaking procedure, where scrutiny for error is 
commonplace and often intense. Similarly, in contrast with their 
customary deference to the legislature’s pohcy choices—at least in cases 
involving only routine economic and social legislation, e.g., WilliamsoTv v.
Lee Optical, 348 U.S. 483 (1955)—courts demand some evidentiary support 
?
for, and a reasoned explanation of, rules adopted by administrators.
This markedly different judicial posture is partly the product of the 
Administrative Procedure Act, which establishes general minimum 
procedures for federal agency rulemaking and expressly contemplates 
some degree of judicial review of the substantive decisions reached by 
administrators. More fundamentally, however, the judicial posture toward 
,’2
agency “legislation” reflects a continuing ambivalence about the political 
legitimacy of pohcy making by administrators. Attenuated pohtical 
accountabihty has promoted legal demands for process transparency and 
substantive rationahty. Administrators may exercise a delegated power to 
legislate, but the legal controls on this “quasi-legislation” are far more 
intrusive than judicial review of legislative actions by legislators.
